title: Upserts: ON CONFLICT, RETURNING and MERGE
summary: Insert-or-update without races: why SELECT-then-INSERT breaks under concurrency, how `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` lets a unique index arbitrate (DO NOTHING, DO UPDATE with `EXCLUDED` and a WHERE), what RETURNING does and does not report, the 'affect row a second time' error, counters and idempotency keys, sequence gaps, and when MERGE is the better tool.
prerequisiteNotes: sql-schema-design: primary keys, UNIQUE constraints (and how they treat NULL) and partial unique indexes. Every upsert is arbitrated by one of those, so you need to know which unique keys a table has before you can write its ON CONFLICT clause.
objectives: Explain why SELECT-then-INSERT races under concurrency and why a transaction alone does not fix it.
Write `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` with DO NOTHING and DO UPDATE, using `EXCLUDED` and the target alias correctly.
Choose a conflict target that matches a unique index: a column list, `ON CONSTRAINT name`, an expression or a partial index with its WHERE.
Make an update conditional with a WHERE on DO UPDATE, and predict exactly which rows RETURNING reports.
Avoid 'cannot affect row a second time' by collapsing a batch to one row per key before upserting.
Use upserts for counters and idempotency keys, explain sequence gaps, and say when MERGE is the better choice.

concepts.title: Why SELECT-then-INSERT races
concepts.body: The classic bug: `SELECT` to see whether a key exists, and `INSERT` if it does not. Two sessions can both run the SELECT before either INSERT commits, so both see nothing and both insert. With a UNIQUE index the loser waits on the winner's uncommitted index entry and then fails with `23505 unique_violation`; without one you silently store a duplicate. Wrapping both statements in a transaction does not help under READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ, because a SELECT cannot lock a row that does not exist yet. The fix is to make the write itself conditional and let the unique index arbitrate: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`. Under the default READ COMMITTED it guarantees, for every proposed row, an insert, an update or a skip: no duplicate and no race error, however many sessions collide.

concepts.title: ON CONFLICT: DO NOTHING, DO UPDATE and EXCLUDED
concepts.body: `ON CONFLICT` is Postgres syntax (SQLite copied it; the SQL standard has MERGE instead). For each proposed row Postgres probes the **arbiter** unique index. No conflict: the row is inserted. Conflict with `DO NOTHING`: the row is skipped without error. Conflict with `DO UPDATE`: the existing row is locked and the SET list runs. Inside SET and WHERE, the stored row is the table name (or the alias from `INSERT INTO t AS alias`) and the proposed row is the special table `EXCLUDED`, with defaults and BEFORE INSERT triggers already applied. Because both have the same columns, an unqualified column on the right of `=` is ambiguous, so always qualify. DO UPDATE needs a conflict target; DO NOTHING may omit it and then skips a conflict on any unique constraint.

concepts.title: The conflict target must match a unique index
concepts.body: The column list in `ON CONFLICT (cols)` is not a filter: Postgres uses it to **infer** an arbiter, a unique index or constraint on exactly those columns (in any order). A plain index cannot arbitrate: `there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification`, raised before any row is written. Other spellings: `ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT name` names a constraint (a bare `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` is not a constraint, so infer it from columns instead); an expression index is targeted by its expression, `ON CONFLICT (lower(email))`; a **partial** unique index needs its predicate repeated, `ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE NOT deleted`. Finally, NULL keys never conflict, because UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct: rows with a NULL key are always inserted unless the column is NOT NULL or the constraint is `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG15+).

concepts.title: Conditional updates and what RETURNING reports
concepts.body: A WHERE on DO UPDATE makes the update conditional, which is how you build 'last write wins': `WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > t.updated_at`. When it is false (or NULL) the row is locked but not changed, and no error is raised. RETURNING lists only rows the statement **wrote**: inserted rows and updated rows. A row skipped by DO NOTHING or by a false WHERE returns nothing, so 'get or create, and give me the id' needs care: a follow-up SELECT can miss a row committed after the statement's snapshot, and the common no-op `DO UPDATE SET key = EXCLUDED.key` always returns the row but writes a new row version every time (bloat, triggers, WAL). To tell inserts from updates, Postgres 18 adds `RETURNING old.*, new.*` (`old` is NULL for an inserted row); older code uses `(xmax = 0) AS inserted`, which leans on internals.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE prices (
  sku        text PRIMARY KEY,
  price      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  updated_at timestamptz   NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('MUG-1', 8.00, '2024-03-05 09:00+00');

INSERT INTO prices AS p VALUES
  ('MUG-1', 7.50, '2024-03-04 09:00+00'),   -- older: ignored
  ('TEE-1', 15.00, '2024-03-04 09:00+00')   -- new: inserted
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET price = EXCLUDED.price, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > p.updated_at
RETURNING new.sku, old.price AS old_price, new.price;   -- PG18
-- TEE-1 | NULL | 15.00     (MUG-1 is not returned)

concepts.title: Duplicate keys in one statement
concepts.body: One INSERT may not update the same target row twice. If the source holds two rows for one key, the second would update a row this command already inserted or updated, and Postgres refuses instead of picking an order: `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`. The whole statement rolls back. DO NOTHING tolerates repeats (the later one is skipped, but which one counts as first depends on the source order), and MERGE has the same rule with its own message. The fix is to decide what two rows for one key mean and collapse the source first: counters add up (`GROUP BY key` with `sum`), snapshots keep the newest (`DISTINCT ON (key) ... ORDER BY key, updated_at DESC`, or `row_number()` = 1), with a tie-breaker so the winner is deterministic.
concepts.code:
-- Fails if a sku appears twice in incoming
INSERT INTO stock AS s (sku, qty)
SELECT sku, qty FROM incoming
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = s.qty + EXCLUDED.qty;
-- ERROR: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time

-- Works: one row per key
INSERT INTO stock AS s (sku, qty)
SELECT sku, sum(qty) FROM incoming GROUP BY sku
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = s.qty + EXCLUDED.qty;

concepts.title: Counters, idempotency keys and sequence gaps
concepts.body: Two everyday upserts. **Counters and rollups**: key the table on the grain (`(tenant_id, day)`) and add instead of overwrite, `SET calls = t.calls + EXCLUDED.calls`; the increment is atomic because the row is locked while it is computed. **Idempotency keys**: the client sends a unique key with a request; the server claims it with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING key`. A row back means this request owns the key and does the work; no row means it is a retry (replay the stored response, answer 409 if the first attempt is still running, or 422 if the payload differs from the stored fingerprint). One side effect to know: defaults such as an identity's `nextval` are computed before the conflict check, so every skipped or updated row still burns a sequence value. Gaps are normal; never treat ids as a count, and use `bigint` for high-churn upsert tables.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key          text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash text NOT NULL,
  status       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'started',
  response     jsonb,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Claim the key: one row back = first time, do the work
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash)
VALUES ('k-42', 'sha256:9f1c...')
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING key;

-- No row back = retry: read what the first attempt stored
SELECT status, request_hash, response
FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = 'k-42';

concepts.title: MERGE, and when to prefer it
concepts.body: `MERGE` (SQL standard, Postgres 15+) joins a source to the target on **any** condition and routes each source row through ordered `WHEN MATCHED [AND ...]` / `WHEN NOT MATCHED [AND ...]` branches that can UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT or DO NOTHING. Postgres 17 adds `RETURNING` with `merge_action()` and `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`, so one statement can also delete or retire target rows missing from a full feed. It needs no unique index, and that is its weakness: MERGE decides 'matched' from its snapshot, so if another session inserts the same key concurrently, the NOT MATCHED branch can fail with a unique violation. Prefer ON CONFLICT for concurrent single-key writes (API upserts, counters, idempotency keys). Prefer MERGE for batch syncs that need deletes, several conditional branches or a non-unique match, ideally with one writer at a time.
concepts.code:
MERGE INTO products AS p
USING product_snapshot AS s ON p.sku = s.sku
WHEN MATCHED AND s.discontinued THEN
  DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > p.updated_at THEN
  UPDATE SET name = s.name, price = s.price, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND NOT s.discontinued THEN
  INSERT (sku, name, price, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.sku, s.name, s.price, s.updated_at)
RETURNING merge_action(), p.sku;   -- PG17+

example:
CREATE TABLE page_views_daily (
  page_id int  NOT NULL,
  day     date NOT NULL,
  views   int  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (page_id, day)
);
INSERT INTO page_views_daily VALUES (1, '2024-03-01', 100);

-- A batch with a repeated key and a new key
WITH batch(page_id, day, views) AS (
  VALUES (1, DATE '2024-03-01', 10),
         (1, DATE '2024-03-01', 5),
         (2, DATE '2024-03-01', 7)
)
INSERT INTO page_views_daily AS v (page_id, day, views)
SELECT page_id, day, sum(views)        -- one row per key first
FROM batch
GROUP BY page_id, day
ON CONFLICT (page_id, day) DO UPDATE
SET views = v.views + EXCLUDED.views   -- add, do not overwrite
RETURNING page_id, views, old.views AS before;   -- PG18 old/new
-- 2 |   7 | NULL  (inserted)
-- 1 | 115 | 100   (updated)

-- Without the GROUP BY:
-- ERROR: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
task: A metering job writes per-tenant API usage into `usage_batch (tenant_id int, day date, calls int, errors int)`. Fold the batch into the rollup table `api_usage_daily (tenant_id int, day date, calls int, errors int)`, whose primary key is `(tenant_id, day)`, with a single statement. A `(tenant_id, day)` that is not in the rollup yet is inserted; one that already exists gets the batch's `calls` and `errors` **added** to its stored values. The batch can contain the same `(tenant_id, day)` several times, even as identical rows, and every row counts. Rows of the rollup that are not in the batch must not change, and an empty batch changes nothing. There is no query to return: the check reads `tenant_id, day, calls, errors` from `api_usage_daily` afterwards.
starter:
-- Fold usage_batch into api_usage_daily: new keys are inserted,
-- existing keys get the batch numbers ADDED. The check reads the table.
INSERT INTO api_usage_daily (tenant_id, day, calls, errors)
SELECT tenant_id, day, calls, errors
FROM usage_batch
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, day) DO UPDATE
SET calls  = EXCLUDED.calls,
    errors = EXCLUDED.errors;
hints: `EXCLUDED.calls` is the incoming number and `u.calls` (with `INSERT INTO api_usage_daily AS u`) is the stored one. A counter adds them: `SET calls = u.calls + EXCLUDED.calls`.

A repeated key in the batch makes DO UPDATE fail with 'cannot affect row a second time'. Insert from `SELECT tenant_id, day, sum(calls), sum(errors) FROM usage_batch GROUP BY tenant_id, day` so each key arrives once. Do not use DISTINCT: identical rows are separate events.
solution:
INSERT INTO api_usage_daily AS u (tenant_id, day, calls, errors)
SELECT tenant_id, day, sum(calls), sum(errors)
FROM usage_batch
GROUP BY tenant_id, day
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, day) DO UPDATE
SET calls  = u.calls  + EXCLUDED.calls,
    errors = u.errors + EXCLUDED.errors;

The grain of the rollup is one row per `(tenant_id, day)`, and that is also its primary key, so it is the natural arbiter: `ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, day)`. The batch is at a finer grain (one row per metering event), so it must be collapsed to the rollup's grain first. That serves two purposes: two batch rows for one key would otherwise make the second update hit a row this statement already touched, which Postgres rejects, and summing is exactly what a counter wants. DISTINCT would be wrong, because two identical rows are two real events. In the DO UPDATE, the alias `u` is the stored row and `EXCLUDED` is the summed batch row, so `u.calls + EXCLUDED.calls` adds rather than overwrites (the starter's `SET calls = EXCLUDED.calls` loses history). New keys take the plain INSERT path with the summed values. An empty batch produces no source rows, so nothing happens. `sum(int)` returns `bigint`, which is assigned back into the `int` columns; a counter that can grow past 2^31 should be `bigint` in the table too.
checklist: The conflict target `(tenant_id, day)` is exactly the table's primary key.
The source is grouped to one row per key with `sum`, not DISTINCT.
DO UPDATE adds the stored and incoming values, with every column reference qualified.
Rows outside the batch keep their values, and an empty batch is a no-op.
pitfalls: Checking existence with SELECT and then inserting from application code: two requests both see nothing and both insert.
Targeting columns that only have a plain (non-unique) index: the statement fails with 'no unique or exclusion constraint matching'.
Forgetting the predicate of a partial unique index in the conflict target, or targeting `(email)` when the index is on `lower(email)`.
Writing `SET n = n + EXCLUDED.n`: a bare `n` is ambiguous between the stored row and EXCLUDED.
Overwriting a counter with `EXCLUDED.count` instead of adding `t.count + EXCLUDED.count`.
Upserting a batch with repeated keys and getting 'cannot affect row a second time'; or deduping with DISTINCT and losing real repeats.
Expecting RETURNING to give back the existing row on DO NOTHING (it returns nothing for skipped rows).
Relying on NULL keys to conflict: NULLs are distinct in a UNIQUE index, so every row with a NULL key is inserted.
Treating identity ids as a row count; every conflict burns a sequence value.
Using MERGE for high-concurrency single-key upserts and being surprised by unique violations from concurrent inserts.

walkthrough.title: Bulk upserts from a staging table
walkthrough.body: For a nightly feed of a few million rows, do not upsert row by row from the application: one round trip per row is slow and every row is its own tiny transaction. Instead `COPY` the file into a staging table (temp or UNLOGGED, no constraints, so a malformed line is something you can query rather than a failed load). Validate and normalise there with SQL. Then run one set-based `INSERT INTO target SELECT ... FROM staging ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... WHERE newer`, after collapsing staging to one row per key. Sort the source by key: two loaders that touch overlapping keys in the same order queue behind each other instead of deadlocking. For very large loads, process key ranges in chunks of a few thousand per transaction so row locks, WAL bursts and replication lag stay bounded. Finish with a RETURNING count (or PG18 `old`/`new`) for the job's metrics, then truncate staging.

walkthrough.title: Writing the counter upsert out loud
walkthrough.body: Start with the grain: 'the rollup has one row per tenant per day, and that pair is the primary key, so it is my arbiter.' Then the source grain: 'the batch has one row per event, so the same key can repeat; I collapse it with GROUP BY and sum, not DISTINCT, because two identical events both count.' Then each outcome: new key, inserted with the sums; existing key, `stored + EXCLUDED`; key not in the batch, untouched. Name the edge cases before the interviewer does: empty batch (no-op), repeated keys (grouped), a key at a month end or on 29 February (dates are just values in the key). Finish with the senior points: the update is atomic because the row is locked, concurrent jobs should feed keys in a consistent order, and a very hot key would be a contention point worth sharding.

walkthrough.title: Get-or-create an id without a race
walkthrough.body: Asked for 'return the tag's id, creating the tag if needed', say why the obvious answers are incomplete. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id` returns nothing when the tag exists. Adding `UNION ALL SELECT id FROM tags WHERE name = $1` in the same statement shares one snapshot, so under READ COMMITTED it can miss a tag that another session committed after the statement started; the robust pattern is to run the SELECT as a separate statement (it gets a new snapshot) and loop if both come back empty. The alternative `ON CONFLICT (name) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name RETURNING id` always returns the id in one statement but writes a new row version on every call, fires update triggers and takes a row lock, which matters for hot rows. Pick the first for read-mostly lookups and the second when simplicity beats write volume.

extraPractice.title: Register new devices and report only those
extraPractice.prompt: Heartbeats arrive in `heartbeats (device_id text, seen_at timestamptz)`. Register every device that is not yet in `devices (device_id text PRIMARY KEY, first_seen timestamptz)`, with `first_seen` set to that device's earliest `seen_at` in the batch. Devices that are already registered must not change, even if the batch has an earlier heartbeat for them. Return `device_id, first_seen` for the newly registered devices only, straight from the INSERT's RETURNING clause. Device ids are case-sensitive, and 'earliest' means the earliest instant.
hints: `ON CONFLICT (device_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING device_id, first_seen` returns exactly the rows that were inserted; skipped ones produce nothing.
Group first: `SELECT device_id, min(seen_at) FROM heartbeats GROUP BY device_id`, so each device is proposed once with its earliest time.
checklist: A device already in `devices` is neither returned nor changed.
A new device with several heartbeats is registered once, at its earliest instant.
The statement does not fail with a unique violation when the batch contains a known device.
extraPractice.solution:
INSERT INTO devices (device_id, first_seen)
SELECT device_id, min(seen_at)
FROM heartbeats
GROUP BY device_id
ON CONFLICT (device_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING device_id, first_seen;

DO NOTHING turns a conflict into a skip, and RETURNING reports only rows the statement wrote, so the result is exactly the newly registered devices. Grouping with `min(seen_at)` proposes each device once with its earliest heartbeat (DO NOTHING would tolerate repeats, but then whichever row came first would win). `timestamptz` compares instants, so `05:00+05` (midnight UTC) is earlier than `01:00+00` on the same date.

extraPractice.title: Last write wins from a feed with duplicates
extraPractice.prompt: A supplier feed lands in `product_feed (feed_id int PRIMARY KEY, sku text, name text, price numeric(10,2), updated_at timestamptz)`. Apply it to `products (sku text PRIMARY KEY, name text, price numeric(10,2), updated_at timestamptz)` in one statement. The feed can hold several versions of one sku: only the one with the latest `updated_at` counts, and if two versions share that latest time, the higher `feed_id` (later arrival) wins. A sku not in `products` is inserted with that version. A sku already in `products` is overwritten (name, price and updated_at) only when the incoming `updated_at` is strictly later than the stored one; otherwise it stays exactly as it is. Skus are case-sensitive. The check reads `sku, name, price, updated_at` from `products`.
hints: Dedupe first or DO UPDATE fails on a repeated sku: `SELECT DISTINCT ON (sku) ... FROM product_feed ORDER BY sku, updated_at DESC, feed_id DESC` keeps the newest version, with feed_id breaking ties.
Put the 'newer only' rule in a WHERE on the DO UPDATE: `WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > p.updated_at` (with `INSERT INTO products AS p`). A false WHERE skips the row silently.
checklist: Each sku is proposed once, chosen by latest `updated_at` then highest `feed_id`.
An incoming row with an equal or older `updated_at` leaves the stored row untouched.
New skus are inserted even when they repeat in the feed.
The statement never raises 'cannot affect row a second time'.
extraPractice.solution:
INSERT INTO products AS p (sku, name, price, updated_at)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (sku) sku, name, price, updated_at
FROM product_feed
ORDER BY sku, updated_at DESC, feed_id DESC
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET name       = EXCLUDED.name,
    price      = EXCLUDED.price,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > p.updated_at;

Two separate rules, applied in two places. Inside the feed, `DISTINCT ON (sku)` with `ORDER BY sku, updated_at DESC, feed_id DESC` keeps one deterministic winner per sku; without the dedupe a repeated sku makes DO UPDATE touch the same row twice and the statement fails, and without the feed_id tie-breaker two runs could pick different winners. Against the table, the WHERE on DO UPDATE compares the winner with the stored row, so an equal or older version is skipped and the stored row is not rewritten (no new row version, no trigger). `timestamptz` compares instants, so `13:00+02` is correctly older than `12:00+00`. The same shape with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY sku ORDER BY updated_at DESC, feed_id DESC) = 1` in a subquery is equally correct and portable.

followUps.question: Two workers upsert overlapping batches into the same table and one of them dies with a deadlock. Why, and what do you change?
followUps.answer: DO UPDATE locks each existing row as it reaches it, in source order. If worker A locks key 1 then needs key 2 while B holds key 2 and needs key 1, Postgres detects the cycle and aborts one with `40P01 deadlock_detected`. Feed keys in a consistent order (`ORDER BY` the key in the INSERT ... SELECT), keep batches small so locks are held briefly, partition work so workers own disjoint key ranges where possible, and retry the aborted transaction, since a deadlock victim is safe to rerun.

followUps.question: A single counter row receives 5,000 increments a second. What happens, and how would you redesign it?
followUps.answer: Every increment takes the same row lock, so writers queue and throughput is capped by one row's commit rate. Each update also writes a new row version (MVCC), so the row churns: lots of WAL and dead tuples for vacuum, mitigated if the update is HOT (no indexed column changed and free space on the page, helped by a lower fillfactor). Fixes: shard the counter (`(key, shard)` with a random shard of 0 to 15, sum on read), buffer increments in the app or a queue and fold them in periodically with one grouped upsert, or append events and roll them up asynchronously. Pick by how fresh the number must be.

followUps.question: MERGE is standard SQL. Why not use it for every upsert?
followUps.answer: MERGE decides matched or not matched from its snapshot. If another session inserts the same key after that, MERGE's INSERT branch hits the unique index and fails with `23505`, whereas ON CONFLICT is built to resolve that race by updating or skipping. So for concurrent single-key upserts (API writes, counters, idempotency keys) ON CONFLICT is the safe primitive. MERGE wins for batch syncs: several conditional branches, DELETE, `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE` (PG17) to retire rows missing from a full snapshot, or a match condition that is not a unique key. Run those with one writer, or catch and retry the unique violation.

followUps.question: Design the idempotency-key table. What if the retry arrives while the first request is still running?
followUps.answer: Columns: the key (primary key, ideally scoped per client: `(client_id, key)`), a fingerprint of the request body, a status (`started`, `done`), the stored response, and `created_at` for expiry. Claim the key in its own short transaction with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` and commit before calling external systems, so a concurrent retry sees the claim. On a conflict: status `done` replays the stored response; `started` returns 409 or a retry-after; a different fingerprint returns 422, since the client reused a key for another request. Expire keys after a window (for example 24 hours) with a batched delete on `created_at`. The side effect itself should carry the key too (pass it to the payment provider) so a crash between charge and save cannot double-charge.

followUps.question: Ids in the table jump from 1041 to 1187. Is that a bug?
followUps.answer: No. Sequences are non-transactional: a value handed out is never given back. ON CONFLICT computes the default (`nextval`) before it knows there is a conflict, so every skipped or updated row burns a value; rolled-back inserts and sequence caching after a crash also leave gaps. Never use ids as a count or assume contiguity. On a high-conflict upsert table this burn rate can exhaust an `int` sequence long before the table has 2 billion rows, so use `bigint`, or avoid drawing a value for rows that will conflict by filtering known keys out in the source first.

followUps.question: The feed is a full snapshot. How do you also remove products that disappeared from it?
followUps.answer: With MERGE on Postgres 17+: `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` (or an UPDATE that sets `active = false`, which is safer for history and foreign keys). With ON CONFLICT, run the upsert and then `DELETE FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staging s WHERE s.sku = p.sku)` in the same transaction. Guard either version: if the snapshot is empty or suspiciously small (a truncated file), abort instead of wiping the table, for example by checking the staging row count against yesterday's first.

takeaways: SELECT-then-INSERT races; let a unique index arbitrate inside the write with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`.
The conflict target must match a unique index or constraint exactly, including a partial index's WHERE or an expression.
In DO UPDATE, the table name or alias is the stored row and `EXCLUDED` is the proposed row; qualify every column.
A WHERE on DO UPDATE gives 'only if newer'; skipped rows, like DO NOTHING conflicts, return nothing from RETURNING.
Collapse the source to one row per key first, or DO UPDATE and MERGE fail with 'cannot affect row a second time'.
Conflicts still burn sequence values; prefer ON CONFLICT for concurrent upserts and MERGE for multi-branch batch syncs.

diagrams.title: SELECT-then-INSERT races; ON CONFLICT does not
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram with session A, session B and Postgres. Both sessions select key K1 and both get zero rows. A inserts K1; B inserts K1 too and has to wait on A's uncommitted index entry. When A commits, B fails with a unique violation. B's retry with INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING succeeds as a no-op with no error.
diagrams.caption: A check in the application only sees the past. Let the unique index arbitrate inside the INSERT itself.

messages.label: 0 rows
messages.note: Both sessions now believe K1 is free. Neither SELECT locked anything: there was no row to lock.

messages.label: INSERT key 'K1'
messages.note: B finds A's uncommitted entry in the unique index and waits for A's transaction to finish.

messages.label: ERROR 23505 unique_violation
messages.note: A committed, so B's row is a duplicate. Without the UNIQUE index both rows would be stored.

messages.label: INSERT 0 0 (no error)
messages.note: Same race, but the conflict is an outcome, not an exception: the row is skipped and the transaction carries on.

diagrams.title: What ON CONFLICT does with each proposed row
diagrams.alt: Decision flow. A proposed row is checked against the arbiter unique index. With no conflict it is inserted and returned. On a conflict with DO NOTHING it is skipped and RETURNING gives no row for it. With DO UPDATE the existing row is locked and the WHERE clause is tested: true updates the row and returns it, false or NULL leaves it unchanged and returns nothing.
diagrams.caption: Three outcomes per row: inserted, updated or skipped. RETURNING only reports the first two.

steps.text: Each proposed row is probed against the **arbiter**: the unique index or constraint that the conflict target names.
No existing row has that key: the row is inserted, exactly like a plain INSERT, and RETURNING reports it.
Conflict with `DO NOTHING`: the row is skipped silently. RETURNING produces nothing for it, so you cannot read the existing id from this statement.
Conflict with `DO UPDATE`: Postgres locks the existing row and evaluates the SET list, where the table name means the stored row and `EXCLUDED` means the proposed one.
The optional WHERE is true: the row is updated and RETURNING reports its new values.
The WHERE is false or NULL: the row stays locked until commit but is not changed, and RETURNING gives nothing for it.

diagrams.title: Duplicate keys inside one upsert
diagrams.alt: Flow. A batch holds two rows for key A and one for key B. Upserting it as is fails with the error that ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE cannot affect a row a second time. Deduplicating first with GROUP BY or DISTINCT ON turns it into one row per key, A with 3 and B with 5, and the upsert then succeeds.
diagrams.caption: One statement may touch each target row once. Collapse the source to one row per key first.

steps.text: Key A appears twice in one statement. The second A would update a row this same command already inserted or updated, so Postgres raises `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time` and the whole statement rolls back.
Decide what two rows for one key mean: counters add up (`GROUP BY key` with `sum`), snapshots keep the latest (`DISTINCT ON (key) ... ORDER BY key, updated_at DESC`).
Now each key appears once and the upsert succeeds. MERGE has the same rule and the same fix.

diagrams.title: An idempotency key absorbs a retry
diagrams.alt: Timeline of a payment request. The client sends a POST with idempotency key k-42. The server claims the key with INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, which returns a row. The card is charged and the response saved on the key row. The response is lost and the client times out, then retries with the same key. The insert now returns no row, so the server replays the stored response and the customer is charged once.
diagrams.caption: The unique key turns "did I already do this?" into an atomic insert. No row back means someone already did.

events.label: Client sends POST /payments with Idempotency-Key k-42
INSERT k-42 ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING key: one row, this request owns k-42
Card is charged; status and response body are saved on the k-42 row
The response is lost on the network and the client times out
Client retries the same request with the same key k-42
The claiming insert returns no row: k-42 exists, so nothing is charged again
Server replays the stored response: one charge, two identical answers

diagrams.title: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT versus MERGE
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. On the left, INSERT ON CONFLICT probes a required unique index: no match inserts, a match updates or skips, and both paths are race-safe per row. On the right, MERGE joins source rows to the target on any condition and routes them to WHEN MATCHED (update or delete) or WHEN NOT MATCHED (insert), but a concurrent insert of the same key can still make it fail with a unique violation.
diagrams.caption: ON CONFLICT is the concurrency-safe insert-or-update. MERGE is the more expressive batch sync.

diagrams.title: Bulk upsert through a staging table
diagrams.alt: Pipeline flow. A feed file is copied into a staging table that has no constraints. A SELECT deduplicates it to one row per key, sorted by key, and feeds a single INSERT ON CONFLICT with a WHERE newer clause into the target table. Large loads are split into chunks of a few thousand keys.
diagrams.caption: Load fast and loose into staging, then dedupe, sort and upsert into the constrained table in one statement per chunk.

steps.text: `COPY` the raw feed into a staging table (temp or UNLOGGED, no constraints) so a bad line does not abort a half-applied load and you can inspect it with SQL.
Collapse to one row per key and sort by key. Dedupe avoids the 'affect row a second time' error; a consistent key order keeps concurrent loaders from deadlocking.
One `INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE newer` applies the whole chunk set-based, not one round trip per row.
For millions of rows, upsert in chunks of a few thousand keys per transaction so row locks and WAL bursts stay small.

exercises.starter:
-- Fold usage_batch into api_usage_daily: new keys are inserted,
-- existing keys get the batch numbers ADDED. The check reads the table.
INSERT INTO api_usage_daily (tenant_id, day, calls, errors)
SELECT tenant_id, day, calls, errors
FROM usage_batch
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, day) DO UPDATE
SET calls  = EXCLUDED.calls,
    errors = EXCLUDED.errors;
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO api_usage_daily AS u (tenant_id, day, calls, errors)
SELECT tenant_id, day, sum(calls), sum(errors)
FROM usage_batch
GROUP BY tenant_id, day
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, day) DO UPDATE
SET calls  = u.calls  + EXCLUDED.calls,
    errors = u.errors + EXCLUDED.errors;
exercises.check: SELECT tenant_id, day, calls, errors FROM api_usage_daily

exercises.starter:
-- Apply product_feed to products: newest feed row per sku, and only
-- overwrite a stored row when the incoming one is strictly newer.
INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price, updated_at)
SELECT sku, name, price, updated_at
FROM product_feed
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET name = EXCLUDED.name,
    price = EXCLUDED.price,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at;
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO products AS p (sku, name, price, updated_at)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (sku) sku, name, price, updated_at
FROM product_feed
ORDER BY sku, updated_at DESC, feed_id DESC
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET name       = EXCLUDED.name,
    price      = EXCLUDED.price,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > p.updated_at;
exercises.check: SELECT sku, name, price, updated_at FROM products

choices: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "tags_pkey"
predict.explain: RETURNING reports only rows the statement actually wrote. The conflicting `(1, 'b')` was skipped, and DO NOTHING does not hand back the existing row, so a get-or-create needs a second lookup (or a no-op DO UPDATE).

choices: ERROR: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "hits_pkey"
predict.explain: The same key appears twice in one statement, so the second row would update a row this command already wrote. Postgres refuses rather than pick an order. Aggregate first: `SELECT k, sum(n) ... GROUP BY k`. (With DO NOTHING the second row would just be skipped.)

choices: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "subs_email_key"
predict.explain: Defaults, including the identity's `nextval`, are computed before the conflict check, so the skipped row still consumed id 2. Sequences never roll back: gaps are normal and ids are not a row count.

Inside DO UPDATE both the stored row and `EXCLUDED` have a `qty`, so a bare `qty` is ambiguous. Qualify it: `SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty` (or use the alias from `INSERT INTO stock AS s`). The target of SET itself is never qualified.

choices: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "prices_pkey"
predict.explain: Version 3 is older than the stored 5, so the WHERE is false: the row is left as it is and nothing is returned. A false WHERE on DO UPDATE is a silent skip, not an error, which is exactly what 'last write wins' needs.

choices: ERROR: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification
ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_pkey"
predict.explain: The conflict target must match a unique index or constraint. A plain index on `email` cannot arbitrate, so the statement fails before inserting anything, even on an empty table. Make the index UNIQUE (or target `(id)`).
Postgres 17 added RETURNING to MERGE, and `merge_action()` says which branch handled each source row. In RETURNING, the target's columns show the new values, so key 1 reports 5 + 2 = 7.

lab.tip: Before writing an upsert, say three things out loud: the unique key that arbitrates it ('the primary key is tenant and day'), what happens on each outcome (new key, existing key, skipped), and whether the source can repeat a key. Interviewers who ask for 'insert or update' are usually probing the race and the duplicate-key case, so name both before they do.
